title: Ericsson CEO: AI Will Drive Next-Gen Network Demand in 2026
summary: Ericsson's new CEO Per Narvinger reveals how AI-powered devices and 6G networks will create unprecedented demand for telecom infrastructure through 2026.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Ericsson's new CEO Per Narvinger predicts AI will fuel massive demand for next-generation telecom networks through custom chip solutions.
- The strategy contrasts with Nokia's Nvidia partnership, betting on purpose-built hardware for 6G rollout by decade's end.
- Emerging applications include satellite integration, indoor coverage, and radar-like sensing for defense and traffic monitoring use cases.


Ericsson's newly appointed CEO Per Narvinger is betting on artificial intelligence to drive unprecedented demand for next-generation telecommunications infrastructure. In his first interview since taking the helm last month, Narvinger outlined a vision where AI-powered devices like smart glasses and connected sensors create exponential growth in data requirements, positioning the Swedish telecom giant for a pivotal role in the transition to 6G networks.


The strategy marks a clear departure from competitor approaches, with Ericsson doubling down on proprietary chip design while rivals like Nokia pursue partnerships with GPU manufacturers. Officially launched on November 9, 2026, this strategic direction sets the stage for how major telecom equipment makers will compete in an AI-driven wireless landscape.


## Custom Chips Versus General-Purpose Hardware


Narvinger's approach centers on Ericsson's custom-designed chips for radio-access networks, arguing they deliver superior cost efficiency compared to using hardware from Nvidia. "In an exponential trend, it's very easy to justify having a special-purpose chip because everyone is trying to break that curve," he explained. This contrasts sharply with Nokia's strategy of expanding into AI data center networking through a partnership that runs Nokia's RAN software on Nvidia architecture.


The Finnish competitor sold a stake to Nvidia in 2025 as part of this collaboration, with Nokia claiming in July that software running on Nvidia's general-purpose chips can improve spectrum efficiency by up to 50% by next year. The competing visions represent fundamentally different bets: Ericsson sees next-generation networks revolving around AI applications on purpose-built hardware, while Nokia favors AI-accelerated networks running on shared infrastructure.


## 6G Rollout and Satellite Competition


Both companies are positioning for a 6G rollout around the end of the decade, with the promise of equipment squeezing more capacity from spectrum at the core of their pitches. Telecom customers are seeking increased efficiency as they brace for new competition from Elon Musk's SpaceX, which has acquired spectrum in the US while expanding from satellites into mobile services.


Rather than viewing satellite operators as pure threats, Narvinger sees opportunity as these players seek to complement their networks with ground-based equipment. He notes that satellite operators currently build equipment largely in-house due to small volumes compared with terrestrial telecoms. However, terrestrial networks will maintain advantages like indoor coverage, a vulnerability Narvinger is addressing by folding Ericsson's private 5G and neutral-host products into its networks division.


## AI-Driven Connectivity and Sensing Applications


The CEO's vision hinges on AI creating even greater value in connectivity as applications become more sophisticated. "There will be even more value in connectivity in the future because AI will be very dependent on the connectivity part," Narvinger said. This dependency extends beyond consumer devices to emerging enterprise and defense applications.


As mobile networking equipment becomes more sophisticated, it can increasingly use communications signals for radar-like sensing, unlocking new applications in defense and traffic monitoring. Key capabilities include:


- Identifying traffic patterns with people and vehicles
- Detecting unauthorized drones in restricted airspace
- Providing seamless indoor connectivity where satellite coverage falters
- Supporting AI workloads requiring low-latency, high-bandwidth connections


## Continuity Amid Industry Challenges


Despite the ambitious AI-focused vision, Narvinger plans to maintain the course charted by predecessor Börje Ekholm, who cut jobs and slashed costs to make Ericsson leaner after years of slow sales. Both Ericsson and Nokia have struggled due to disappointing 5G demand, falling short of the wireless revolution once promised by the technology.


The 52-year-old Ericsson veteran, who previously ran the company's networks division, is betting that AI will provide the catalyst that 5G deployment alone could not deliver. His first moves as CEO signal this priority, reorganizing internal divisions to strengthen offerings as AI increases demand for seamless connectivity across satellite, terrestrial, and indoor environments.


## What This Means


Ericsson's AI-centric strategy represents a high-stakes wager that purpose-built hardware will outperform general-purpose solutions in the coming wave of network upgrades. As telecom operators prepare for 6G deployment and face new competition from satellite providers, the choice between custom chips and flexible platforms will shape infrastructure investments worth billions. For enterprises evaluating connectivity partners, understanding these competing approaches becomes critical as AI workloads demand ever-greater network performance. The vision also opens new markets in sensing and defense applications, potentially diversifying revenue streams beyond traditional telecom equipment sales.
